paragraphs.text:
ORATION ON PULCHERIA

I do not know how I am to handle this speech. I see that my subject is twofold, and grievous on both counts, so that whichever of the two it takes up, it will not be easy for my speech to go forward without tears. The present turn of the year, as our shepherd announced to us yesterday, brings back the memory of the grievous events that once befell the neighbouring city through the earthquake. Who could recount those without tears? And this great and illustrious city, the fairest of cities, set above every other under the sun, has suffered another earthquake, and has been stripped of no small ornament. The light that shone in her has been suddenly taken away, to be added to the good fortune of the royal house in heaven, and for this reason the city shares the gloom of our sovereigns. You who fill this assembly are certainly not unaware of what I mean, since you see both this very place in which we are gathered and the gloom that fills it. So I do not know which earthquake to turn my speech to, the present one or the one that happened long ago. Or perhaps it is right to stand firm against the greater of the two griefs, and to soothe the city's own pain by applying some reasoning to the wound like a remedy. For even if not all who share in this misfortune are present at the gathering, the speech will perhaps reach through those who are present to those who are not.

For those physicians are wise who use their skill to stand against the worst of the pains, and put off treating the less severe ones. Those who are expert in these matters say that if two pains fall on one body at the same time, only the greater is felt, since the lesser is hidden away by the force of the pain that prevails. That is how I see the present case. Our new grief, which is our own, is stronger than the griefs that pain us through memory. How could anyone not be moved by what has happened? Who has a soul so unfeeling? Who has a character so made of iron that he could take this event without pain? You all surely know this young dove who was being raised in the royal nest, who was just growing her shining feathers yet surpassed her years in her graces: how she has left the nest and is gone, how she has flown away out of our sight, how envy has suddenly snatched her from our hands. Or should we call her not a dove but a fresh-blooming flower, which had not yet shone forth fully from its bud, but part of it was already shining and part was hoped to shine; and yet even small and unfinished as it was, it outshone everything. How suddenly it was quenched within its bud, and before it came to its prime and spread its fragrance through the whole flower, it withered in upon itself and became dust! No one plucked it, no one wove it into a garland; nature laboured in vain. Its goodness lay in hopes, but envy fell on it sideways like a sword and cut the hope short. What happened, brothers, was truly an earthquake, an earthquake no more merciful than any other grievous calamity. It did not ruin the lifeless beauty of buildings, nor throw to the ground richly coloured paintings or splendid works of stone; this earthquake fell suddenly on the very building of nature, bright with beauty and flashing with graces, and brought it down. I saw the lofty sapling too, the tall-crowned palm (I mean the imperial power), which with its royal virtues, as with branches, rises above the whole world and embraces all things. I saw him, who rules over others, bowed by nature and bending down at the loss of the flower. I saw also the noble vine that is wrapped around the palm, she who bore this flower for us, and what pangs she suffered a second time, in her soul, not in her body, when this shoot was plucked from her. Who passed through this grief without groaning? Who did not lament this loss to our life? Who did not let fall tears at this sorrow? Who did not mingle his own voice with the common chorus of lament? I saw a sight that I can vouch for, yet one that those who take in wonders by hearsay would not believe.

I saw a sea of people, standing so densely packed that it appeared to the eyes like water on every side. The church was full; the forecourt of the church was full; so was the square beyond, the streets, the middle, the sides, and the open space on the rooftops. Everything one could see was a mass of people, as though the whole world had run together to one place for this grief. And the spectacle set before all was that holy flower, borne on a golden bier. How downcast were the faces of all who looked on! How wet with tears their eyes! Hands beaten one against another, and groans besides that betrayed the anguish in their hearts! It did not seem to me at that hour (and perhaps not to the others then present either) that the gold gleamed with its natural grace; rather the brilliance of the gems, the cloths woven with gold, the sparkle of the silver, and the light of the fire, plentiful and abundant, stretched out along both sides in an unbroken line of wax torches, all were darkened together by the mourning, and all shared in the common gloom. Then great David too lent his own hymns to the laments, and exchanging his bright choral dance for one of wailing and mourning, he called forth lamentations with his songs. At that time every pleasure had been driven from people's souls, and the only pleasure left them was in tears.

Since, then, reason has been so overcome by grief, it is time to restore, as far as possible, the weariness of our minds through the counsel of reason. For there is no small danger that, if we disregard the Apostle's words in this matter, we shall be condemned along with those who have no hope. For he says, as we heard just now from the reader, that we must not grieve for those who have fallen asleep, since this grief belongs only to those who have no hope. But someone of a fainter spirit might say, I suppose, that the divine Apostle commands what is impossible, and that his injunctions go beyond nature. For how can one who lives within nature rise above grief and not be overcome by sorrow at such a sight, when death does not come in its due season in old age, but in earliest youth the bloom is quenched by death, the ray of the eyes is covered by the eyelids, the flush of the cheek turns to pallor, the mouth is held fast in silence, the flower of the lips darkens, and this seems hard not only to the parents but to everyone who looks on the grief? What, then, shall we say to these people? We will not speak our own word, brothers, but will set before them the saying read to us from the Gospel. For you heard the Lord say: “Let the little children be, and do not hinder them from coming to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven.” [?] So then, even if your child has gone away from you,

she has run to the Master. She has closed her eye to you, but opened it to the eternal light. She has left your table, but been added to the table of the angels. The plant has been uprooted from here, but planted in paradise. She has passed from a kingdom to a kingdom. She has put off the flower of the purple, but put on the robe of the kingdom above. Shall I tell you the material of that divine garment? It is not linen, nor wool, nor threads spun by silkworms. Hear David, who tells from what God's garments are woven: “You have clothed yourself with praise and majesty, wrapping yourself in light as in a cloak.” Do you see what she has received in exchange for what? Does it grieve you that the beauty of her body is no longer seen? That is because you do not see the true beauty of her soul, which now rejoices in the festival of heaven. How beautiful is that eye which sees God! How sweet the mouth adorned with divine hymns! For it says: “Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babes you have perfected praise.” How beautiful the hands that never did evil! How lovely the feet that never trod in wickedness, nor set their step in the way of sinners! How beautiful the whole countenance of that soul, adorned not with the gleam of gems but shining with simplicity and innocence!

But perhaps it grieves you that she did not reach old age. Tell me, what good do you see in old age? Is it good for the eyes to smart, for the cheek to wrinkle, for the teeth to fall from the mouth and make the tongue lisp, for the hand to tremble, for one to stoop toward the ground, to limp on one's feet, to lean on those who lead one by the hand, to wander in one's mind and ramble in one's speech, as necessarily happens at that age? And are we indignant over this, that she did not come to experience such things? Surely we ought rather to rejoice with those whose life has not admitted the experience of grievous things, who have felt nothing painful here and will know nothing grievous there. For such a soul, having nothing for which to come to judgement, does not fear Gehenna, is not afraid of judgement; it remains fearless and undismayed, since no consciousness of evil brings on it the fear of judgement. “But,” someone says, “she ought to have come to full age and been made radiant in the bridal chamber.” But the true Bridegroom will answer you that the heavenly bridal bower is better, and that chamber more precious, in which there is no fear of widowhood. Tell me, then, what good things has she been deprived of by putting off this fleshly life? Shall I tell you the good things of life? Griefs and pleasures, angers and fears, hopes and desires: these and the like are what we are entangled with in this present life. What harm, then, has she suffered who has been set free from so many tyrants? For every passion, when it gains the upper hand, becomes a tyrant over our soul and enslaves our reason. Or does it grieve us that she was not worn down by

the pangs of childbirth, that she was not crushed by the cares of raising children, that she did not endure the same pains that her parents have endured over her? But such things deserve congratulation, not lamentation. For to have come into no evil at all is something better than human nature allows. So too wise Solomon, in his own book of Scripture, calls the departed more blessed than the living. And great David says that our life in the flesh deserves lament and wailing. And yet both of these men, though illustrious in their kingship and having at their command a share in all the pleasures of life, were in no way drawn to present enjoyment; rather, because they desired the ineffable goods laid up in the bodiless life, they counted life in the flesh a misfortune. I have heard David in many places in the sacred Psalms longing to be free of this constraint, where he says now, “My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord,” and now, “Bring my soul out of prison.” Likewise Jeremiah too judges worthy of a curse the day that began this life for him. And one can find many such sayings of the saints of old recorded in divine Scripture, men who were weighed down by life in the flesh out of desire for the life that is truly life.

So too great Abraham once eagerly brought his beloved son to God as a sacrifice, knowing that the boy's departure would be to something better and more divine. Those of you who are familiar with the story are surely not unaware of the accounts about him. For what does Scripture say? That when Abraham was young, a promise came to him from God about a son; but when he had passed his prime and was already withered by time, when nature stops increasing itself and old age no longer answers to its impulses, then, beyond all human hope, the promise was brought to fulfilment, and the child Isaac was born. When a fitting length of time had passed and he had shot up like a sapling in beauty and stature, he was sweet to his parents' eyes, shining with the beauty of youth. Then came to Abraham the testing and trial of his soul, whether he could truly discern what is better in the nature of things, whether he was not looking only to the present life. And God said to him: “Offer up your son as a sacrifice, as a whole burnt offering.” All of you who are fathers and have children, and have been taught by nature to love your offspring, surely know how Abraham would likely have felt if he looked only to the present life, if he were a slave of nature, if he reckoned the sweetness of life to lie in this present existence. But why speak of him, and pass over his wife, the weaker part of human nature? If she too had not been taught the more divine things by her husband, if she had not known that the hidden life is better than the visible one, she would not have allowed her husband to do such a thing to the child. She would surely have been stirred by a mother's heart and thrown herself around

her child, and wrapping him in her arms, would have taken the fatal blow in his place. Would she not have said these words to Abraham: “Spare the boy, husband! Do not become an evil tale for the world; let us not become a fable for later ages. Do not begrudge your son his life; do not rob him of the sweet sunlight. A bridal chamber is what fathers seek for their children, not a tomb; a wedding crown, not a murderous sword; a nuptial torch, not a funeral fire. These are things that robbers and enemies do, not the hands of fathers to their children. But if the evil must happen at all, let not Sarah's eye see Isaac put to death. See, thrust the sword through us both, beginning with me, wretched woman; one blow will suffice for the two of us. Let one mound be raised over us both; let one gravestone tell the tragedy of our common misfortune.” Sarah would surely have said these things and others like them, had she not seen with her eyes the things that are invisible to us. For she knew that the end of life in the flesh becomes, for those who depart, the beginning of a more divine life. The one who departs leaves shadows behind and lays hold of truth; he leaves behind deceits and errors and tumults, and finds those good things that are beyond eye and ear and heart. Neither love will torment him, nor will filthy desire [?] him, nor will pride puff him up; nor will any other of the passions that grieve the soul trouble him, but God becomes all things to him. That is why he gives his son to God so eagerly.

And what of great Job? When he had been suddenly stripped of all his possessions, and before he could gather his soul after the earlier blows, the last blow was announced to him: how did he take the [?] concerning his children? He had three daughters and seven sons, and he was blessed in his fine children. For though they were so many, they were all one in their love for one another. They did not live each apart by himself, but all visited one another, and through their round of hospitality they continually delighted one another in turn and were delighted. And on that day, too, it was the eldest brother's turn to hold the banquet. The mixing bowls were full, the table full of food, the cups in their hands; there were also, as one would expect, sights to see and music to hear, and every delight of a feast; all of one mind, with kindnesses, games and smiles, everything that young people gathered at a hearth would naturally enjoy. What happened then? At the height of their enjoyment of these pleasures the roof was shaken down upon them, and the banquet became the tomb of the ten children. The mixing bowl was mingled with the blood of the young, and the food was defiled with the gore of their bodies. When such a calamity was announced to Job (look at the athlete, I beg you, through my words, not only so that you may admire the victor, for the gain from admiration is small, but so that you may emulate the man in like circumstances, and that he may become your trainer

[?] with his nails, or tearing out the hair of his head, or sprinkling dust over himself, or beating his breast with his hands, or throwing himself to the ground, or surrounding himself with mourners, or calling out the names of the departed and wailing over [?]? He did none of these things. The messenger of evil told of the calamity that had befallen the children; Job heard it, and at once began to reflect philosophically on the nature of things: from where things come, by whom they are brought into being, and who should rightly have charge of them. “The Lord gave, [?] the Lord has taken away.” From God, he says, comes to human beings [?] their coming into being, and to him is their dissolution; whatever something has been brought forth from, into that it is also dissolved. God, then, who has the power to give, likewise has the power to take away. Being good, he plans what is good; being wise, he knows what is beneficial. As it pleased the Lord (and it certainly pleased him rightly), so he has done. May [?]

Do you see how lofty was the athlete's greatness of soul? He turned the time of affliction into an occasion for philosophical reflection on the nature of things. For he knew well that the life that is truly life is laid up for us in hope, while the present life is, as it were, the seed of the life to come. What we hope for differs from what is present as much as the ear of grain differs from the seed from which it springs. The present life corresponds to the seed; the life we hope for is shown in the beauty of the ear of grain. For this perishable body must put on imperishability, and this mortal body must put on immortality. Looking to these things, Job rejoices with his children in their good fortune, since they had been released the sooner from the bonds of life. And here is the proof: when God's promise pledged double in return for everything that had been taken away, and the repayment was doubled in everything else, he did not seek the doubling for his children alone; only ten were given in place of the ten taken away. Since human souls abide forever, it is for this reason that he receives double recompense for the things that perished; but in the case of the children, those born afterwards are counted together with those born before, since all are alive to God, and temporary death in no way prevents the departed from existing. For death is nothing else for human beings but a cleansing from wickedness. For since our nature was originally fashioned by the hand of the God of all as a kind of vessel to receive good things,

but the enemy of our souls poured evil into us by deceit, the good had no room left. For this reason, so that the evil that has grown into us may not last forever, by a higher providence the vessel is dissolved for a time by death, so that once the evil has drained away, humanity may be refashioned and restored, unmixed with evil, to the life it had in the beginning. For this is the resurrection: the restoration of our nature to its original state. If, then, our nature cannot be restored to something better without resurrection, and resurrection cannot take place unless death goes before it, then death would be a good thing, since it becomes for us the beginning and the road of our change for the better. Let us therefore cast out, brothers, our grief for those who have fallen asleep, a grief which only those who have no hope endure. And our hope is Christ, to whom be glory and power, honour and worship, for ever and ever.
